claim: For every \(0<\rho<1/2\), there exists a compactly supported absolutely continuous probability measure \(\mu_\rho\) on \(\mathbb R\), supported in \([1/2,5/2]\), such that \(|\widehat{\mu_\rho}(\xi)|\le C_\rho(1+|\xi|)^{-\rho}\) for every \(\xi\in\mathbb R\), yet its dyadic lacunary maximal operator \(M_{\mu_\rho}f(x)=\sup_{k\in\mathbb Z}|f*(\mu_\rho)_k(x)|\) is unbounded from \(H^1(\mathbb R)\) to \(L^{1,\infty}(\mathbb R)\).

correctness.rationale: The point-selection lemma follows from Hoeffding's inequality on an O(N^4)-point grid and the uniform derivative bound. With bump radius epsilon N^{-1-b}, the exact sinc formula gives decay exponent alpha=1/[2(1+b)] with a logarithmic factor. Choosing b so rho<alpha gives the claimed rho-decay. The finite-scale atom argument remains valid on theta L<=k<=bL; in the mixture, earlier components are suppressed by 2^{-k}||K_{N_l}||_infinity and later components are controlled by an L1 tail estimate, yielding weak-L1 quasi-norms growing like q^{m+1}.

originality.rationale: The closest primary source proves endpoint failure with exponent 1/8 and expressly does not claim that exponent optimal. The present construction retunes the concentration threshold and bump radius to reach every exponent below 1/2. Targeted database and primary-literature comparisons found no same-object statement of this stronger decay range; this is not treated as proof of exhaustive novelty.
residual_risks: No exhaustive historical-priority claim is made; absence of an exact match in semantic-search results is not proof of novelty.
The construction is one-dimensional and the measure depends on the target exponent rho through the parameters a, b and q.
The endpoint rho=1/2 is not reached, and the argument does not establish any optimality statement at or above that exponent.
The centers are selected existentially rather than by an explicit deterministic algorithm.

value.rationale: Fourier decay exponent is the main quantitative parameter in the decay-only endpoint question. Improving from 1/8 to every exponent below 1/2 substantially narrows the unknown range and approaches the natural Plancherel threshold, while the same measure still fails the endpoint bound. The primary paper explicitly leaves the optimal decay range open.
